unit.unitOverview: Communication means presenting information so that others can understand it, by speaking or writing, and also listening carefully to others and asking good questions. It has two halves that always work together: presenting your ideas clearly, and listening so you truly understand what others say back.

explainers.title: Hello, and welcome to your final unit
explainers.body:
Hello, and welcome to the last unit of your Global Perspectives year at Ehel Academy. You have travelled a long way. This year you have grown all six thinking skills, one at a time, and here they all are together:

This unit is about that sixth and final skill: Communication. It is a wonderful skill to end with, because it is where all your other work finally goes out into the world. You can research an issue carefully, analyse it, judge it, reflect on it and work on it with a team, but none of that helps anyone else until you can share it clearly. Communication is how your good thinking reaches other people and makes a difference.

Why does communication matter beyond school? Think about the grown-ups around you. A nurse explaining how to keep a wound clean. A community leader trying to persuade the town to fix a dangerous road. All of them are communicating: presenting information clearly, and listening to the people who answer back. A learner who practises this now will be heard, and able to help others, for the whole of their life.
bullets: Research — finding out about the world in a careful, organised way.
Analysis — breaking a topic into parts and asking why things happen.
Evaluation — deciding how strong an idea or a piece of evidence really is.
Reflection — thinking about how you learn and how you have changed your mind.
Collaboration — working well together with other people.
Communication — sharing your ideas clearly so that others understand you.

explainers.title: So what is communication?
explainers.body:
Many people think communication just means talking. It is more than that. Communication means presenting information so that others can understand it, whether you speak it or write it. It also means listening to others when they present, and asking good questions so that you understand them. So communication always has two halves that work together.

A good communicator is strong at both halves. If you only present, you miss what others know and cannot answer their questions; if you only listen, your own good ideas stay locked inside your head. This unit grows both halves, so you can share an issue and truly discuss it.
bullets: Presenting — sending your ideas out clearly, by speaking or writing, so that a listener or reader can follow them.
Listening — taking in what others send you, by listening or reading, and asking questions when something is not clear.

explainers.title: How you will learn this unit
explainers.body:
You are learning in the Ehel Academy way, which means three kinds of support work together:

In the old style of this subject, learners were told to 'present to the class', 'talk to a partner', or 'discuss as a group'. In our model, you do something even better. First you rehearse with your AI tutor, as many times as you like. The tutor will listen to your presentation, play the part of your audience, ask you the awkward questions a real listener might ask, argue the other side so you can practise answering, and give you kind, honest feedback. Then, when you are ready, you deliver it for real: to your teacher in your twice-weekly session, and to your family or community at home.

Every time you see an 'Ask Your AI Tutor' box in this unit, treat it as a real rehearsal, and every time you see a 'Deliver it for real' box, treat it as your moment to be heard.

Your communication skills grow in three stages, just as every skill did this year: you start each one, then develop it, then get better at it. Do not worry if presenting feels scary at first. Almost everyone feels that way, and rehearsing with your tutor is exactly how the fear shrinks.
bullets: You, at your own pace. You read, think and complete the activities in your own time. You can slow down on a hard idea, or move quickly through an easy one.
Your AI tutor, ready any time, day or night. In this unit your AI tutor has a special job: it is your audience and your rehearsal partner.
Your teacher, about twice a week. In your live sessions you deliver your best work for real, to a real audience, and get to know the other learners.

explainers.title: Meet Mina, who brings it all together
explainers.body:
All year we have followed learners at Ehel Academy in Hargeisa. For this final unit, meet Mina, who is about to pull a whole year of thinking together.

Since the start of the year, Mina has been working on one Challenge: the busy, smoky road outside her school, and how children get to school each morning. She researched it, counting cars and surveying her class. She analysed it, mapping the causes of the traffic and its consequences for health and safety. She evaluated her sources and listened to different families' perspectives. She reflected on how her own opinion changed. And she collaborated with a small team to plan what could help. Now Mina has one job left, and it is the most important of all: she must communicate what she has found, so that her school and her community will actually do something about it.

Mina's plan is to present a clear, fair and persuasive case: that more children at Ehel Academy should walk or cycle to school instead of coming by car, so that the air is cleaner and the street is safer. As you meet each new communication skill, you will watch exactly how Mina builds and delivers her case. By the end, she will stand up in front of real people and be heard. You will be doing the very same thing, with a Challenge that matters to you.

explainers.title: Your Challenge: communicating what matters
explainers.body:
Your Challenge for this unit is to communicate an issue you care about so clearly and so fairly that others understand it and want to help. You will build a short presentation or discussion, rehearse it with your AI tutor, and deliver it for real. Here are three good issues to communicate about. Any of them could be your Challenge:

Your classmates will care about different things. Leila wants to protect the turtles she once saw hatching at Berbera. Omar thinks the school rule about bicycles is unfair. Nadia wants cleaner air on her walk to school. Any of these could grow into a strong Challenge to communicate.

You do not have to choose this very moment. As you meet each skill, keep a note of any issue you would love other people to understand and act on. That feeling, wanting to be heard about something that matters, is the heart of communication.
bullets: Walking or cycling to school. Should more children travel to school on foot or by bicycle, for cleaner air and safer streets, instead of coming by car? This is Mina's Challenge, and a strong one for a persuasive case.
Protecting local wildlife. Should a nesting beach for the sea turtles on the Berbera coast be protected by a new rule? This has clear arguments for and against.

A local rule or fairness issue. Is there a rule at your school or in your town that you think should change, or a new rule that would make things fairer? Presenting a case about a rule is exactly what communication is for.

explainers.title: Starting: presenting clearly and listening well
explainers.body: The first two skills are the foundation of everything else. They are the two halves of communication in their simplest form: telling others about an issue, and listening to what they tell you back.

explainers.title: Skill 1: Presenting information clearly
explainers.body:
To present means to share information with other people so that they understand it. You can present by speaking, such as giving a short talk, or by writing, such as writing a clear paragraph. The goal is always the same: the person on the other side should end up understanding your idea just as you do.

Three simple habits make any presentation clearer:
bullets: Start by saying what your issue is, so your audience knows what you are talking about before you dive in.
Take one idea at a time, in a sensible order, instead of jumping about.
Use examples, because a real example makes an idea easy to picture and remember.

explainers.title: Skill 2: Telling others about an issue, and listening so you understand
explainers.body:
Real communication is a two-way street. You tell others about your issue, and you listen to what they tell you, and when something is unclear you ask a question. Listening well is a skill in itself: it means paying full attention, making notes of the important parts, and asking about anything you did not catch.

Many issues have two sides, with arguments for and arguments against. An argument is a reason someone gives to support their view. When people share their arguments and listen to each other's, everyone understands the issue far better than they did alone.

explainers.title: Developing: building a clear, persuasive case
explainers.body: Now you move from simply telling and listening to building a case: choosing your strongest arguments, planning a clear structure, referring to your sources, and using language that persuades, all while thinking about the people you want to reach.

explainers.title: Skill 3: Finding the arguments and evidence in a source
explainers.body:
Before you can present a good case, you need good material. A useful skill is to read a source, such as an article or a leaflet, and pull out its arguments and the supporting evidence for each one. An argument is the reason; the supporting evidence is the fact, detail or example that backs it up. A strong argument always has support; a weak one is just a claim with nothing behind it.

A neat way to do this is to make two columns: one for each argument you find, and one for the supporting ideas or examples beside it.

explainers.title: Skill 4: Choosing your most persuasive arguments
explainers.body:
You will usually find more arguments than you can use. A good communicator selects only the strongest ones, because a few powerful arguments persuade far better than a long list of weak ones. To be persuasive means to be good at making other people agree with you or take action.

What makes an argument persuasive to an audience? Usually three things:
bullets: It has strong support behind it, such as a clear fact or a real example, so it is hard to dismiss.
It matters to the audience, touching something they care about, such as their health, their money or their children.
It is easy to picture, so the audience can imagine it and remember it afterwards.

explainers.title: Skill 5: Making a skeleton plan
explainers.body:
A presentation without a plan wanders, and a wandering talk loses its audience. So before you write or speak, you make a skeleton plan: a simple frame that shows the order of your ideas, like the bones that hold a body upright. A well-tested skeleton for a persuasive case has five parts, in this order:

Notice the clever shape. You do not hide the other side; you include one honest argument against in the middle, then answer it with another argument for. This makes your case fairer and, oddly, more convincing, because your audience can see you have thought about both sides.
bullets: Introduction — say what the issue is, and where you stand.
Argument for (+) — your first strong reason in favour.
Argument against (-) — the other side's best point, fairly stated.
Argument for (+) — another strong reason in favour, to answer the other side.
Conclusion — sum up and say clearly what you want to happen.

explainers.title: Skill 6: Presenting with a clear structure, and referring to your sources
explainers.body:
Your skeleton plan gives your presentation its structure, the clear beginning, middle and end that lets a listener follow you without getting lost. When you present, you can even signal your structure out loud, with phrases like 'First,' 'On the other hand,' and 'So, to sum up.' These little signposts tell your audience exactly where they are.

A strong presenter also refers to sources. When you use a fact, you say where it came from. This does two things: it proves you are not just making things up, and it lets your audience trust and check your work. You can refer to a source in a simple, spoken way.
bullets: According to a health website, dirty air can make it harder to breathe.
In my own survey of twenty classmates, most came to school by car.
A road-safety officer told me that a marked crossing makes a road much safer.

explainers.title: Skill 7: Stating your position and using persuasive language
explainers.body:
A persuasive presenter makes their position clear: they say where they stand on the issue. A helpful way to think about your position is to place it on a scale, from strongly in favour to strongly against:

Once you know your position, you can explain it in a structured way, using linking words to stack up your reasons: 'I am strongly in favour of this. This is mainly because ... In addition ... Furthermore ... Finally ...'. Those linking words carry your audience smoothly from one reason to the next.

You can also choose persuasive language: words and phrases that gently move your audience to agree or to act. Used honestly, they make your case vivid and strong.
bullets: Strongly in favour — In favour — Neutral — Against — Strongly against.
Paint a picture: 'Imagine a street where children walk safely and the air is clean.'
Include the audience: 'Surely we all want our younger brothers and sisters to breathe clean air.'
Call for action: 'It is time to act, and the first step is simple.'

explainers.title: Skill 8: Thinking about your audience
explainers.body:
Your audience is the people you are presenting to, and a clever communicator always asks: who am I trying to influence, and what do they already care about? To influence someone means to change how they think or what they do. Different audiences care about different things, so the same case can be told in different ways.

You do not change your facts for different audiences; you change which arguments you lead with, and which examples you choose, so that your case connects with what that audience cares about most.

explainers.title: Skill 9: Structuring so your listener grasps the key message
explainers.body:
There is a difference between saying everything you know and helping a listener pick out the key message. A good structure does the second. If you organise your talk well, a listener could sketch the shape of it afterwards: here was the issue, here were the reasons, here was the conclusion. That is the test of a clear structure.

Two habits help your listener enormously:
bullets: Group similar points together, instead of scattering them, so each part of your talk has one job.
Say your key message twice: once near the start, and once again in your conclusion, so nobody misses it.

explainers.title: Skill 10: Writing your introduction, body and conclusion
explainers.body: When you write your case out in full, your skeleton plan grows into three clear parts: an introduction, some body paragraphs, and a conclusion. Each part has its own job.
bullets: The introduction names the issue and states your position, and it should grab the audience's attention.
The body paragraphs give your arguments, one main idea per paragraph, each with its supporting evidence.
The conclusion sums up your case and says clearly what you want to happen next.

explainers.title: Skill 11: Using facts and opinions, and acknowledging the other side
explainers.body:
A believable case is built from both facts and opinions, and a good communicator knows the difference. A factual claim is something that can be checked against reliable evidence. An opinion is what someone thinks or believes, which others may disagree with. You need both: facts make your case solid, and opinions show what you believe and why it matters.

The most convincing communicators do one more brave thing: they acknowledge the other side. They say, honestly, what people who disagree might argue, and then they answer it. Far from weakening your case, this makes your audience trust you more, because you are clearly being fair.
bullets: Fact: Cars give off exhaust fumes. This can be checked, so it is a fact.
Opinion: Walking to school is the best way to travel. This is a belief, so it is an opinion.

explainers.title: Getting better: listening and asking relevant questions
explainers.body: The final skill returns to the second half of communication: listening. A skilled communicator is not only a clear speaker but a sharp, generous listener who asks relevant questions, the kind that help everyone understand an issue more deeply.

explainers.title: Skill 12: Active listening and asking relevant questions
explainers.body:
Active listening means listening with full attention, on purpose. You watch the speaker, you follow their argument, and you note the parts you want to ask about. Then, when they finish, you respond with a relevant question: one that is truly about what they said, and that helps you understand or test their idea. Three kinds of question are especially useful:

Good questions are a gift to a speaker, not an attack. Asking 'How do you know that?' kindly helps the speaker show their evidence, and helps the whole group decide how much to trust the idea. If an answer is still unclear, you ask a gentle follow-up to clarify: 'Can you tell me a little more about that?'
bullets: To understand: Could you explain what you mean by that?
To go deeper: What do you mean by a 'safe' crossing, exactly?
To test the idea: How do you know that? Where did that fact come from?

explainers.title: How communication draws on all five earlier skills
explainers.body:
Communication is the last skill for a reason: it gathers up every skill you have grown this year and sends them out into the world. Look how each earlier skill lives inside a good presentation:

So communication is not a brand-new skill sitting on its own. It is the moment all six skills work together. Every hour you spent researching, analysing, evaluating, reflecting and collaborating this year now pays off, because it is the strong thinking behind a message worth hearing.
bullets: Research gives you the facts and sources you refer to, so your case is believable and not just a feeling.
Analysis gives you the arguments, causes and consequences that make up the body of your case.
Evaluation helps you judge which arguments and sources are strong enough to use, and which to drop.
Reflection helps you notice how your own view has changed, and answer the question 'why do you think that?' honestly.
Collaboration taught you to listen to others and value their perspectives, which is the whole second half of communicating.

explainers.title: Putting it all together: communicating a whole Challenge
explainers.body: You have now met every communication skill in this unit. Here is how they fit together into one smooth path you can follow to communicate any Challenge:
bullets: Choose your issue and decide your position on it.
Read your sources and pull out the arguments and their supporting evidence.
Select your most persuasive arguments.
Build a skeleton plan: introduction, argument for, argument against, argument for, conclusion.
Think about your audience and who you want to influence.
Write your introduction, body paragraphs and conclusion, using facts, opinions and persuasive language.
Acknowledge the other side fairly, and refer to your sources.
Rehearse with your AI tutor, then deliver it for real to your teacher and your community.
Listen to the questions people ask, and answer them, asking your own relevant questions in return.

explainers.title: You have completed your Year 6 skills journey
explainers.body:
Look back at how far you have come this year. You began by learning to research the world carefully. You learned to analyse an issue into its causes and consequences, to evaluate how strong different ideas and sources really are, to reflect honestly on your own learning, and to collaborate kindly and well with a team. And now, with communication, you have learned to share all of that clearly and fairly, and to be heard.

These six skills are yours to keep. They are not just for Global Perspectives, or even for school. They are the skills of a thoughtful, fair and useful person: someone who finds things out, thinks them through, works well with others, and speaks up for what matters. You will use them for the rest of your life.

Well done for finishing your Year 6 journey. Be proud of the thinker you have become, and get ready to grow these six skills even further in the years ahead. The world needs young people who can research the truth, think clearly, work together, and communicate with honesty and care. This year, you have started to become exactly that.

bigIdeas.title: One big idea to remember
lines: In Global Perspectives, the topic is like a bus, and the skill is where the bus takes you.
We will use real-world topics such as walking to school, clean air and protecting sea turtles.
But the real prize is not the topic. It is to become a clear, fair communicator who could present almost any idea, and listen well to almost anyone.

bigIdeas.title: The two halves of communication
lines: Presenting: How can I share my ideas so that others understand them clearly?
Listening: When others present, what questions can I ask to understand them better?
Every strong communicator keeps swapping between these two halves, like a good game of catch.

bigIdeas.title: Being fair to every perspective
lines: In any community, people hold different views, shaped by their family, work and beliefs.
One family drives because the walk feels unsafe; another longs for cleaner air; a shopkeeper worries about fewer customers.

A fair communicator represents these perspectives honestly, even the ones they disagree with, and never pretends a whole community thinks one way. Listening evenly to all sides is at the heart of Global Perspectives.

bigIdeas.title: Your Challenge runs through everything
lines: Choose one issue you would love other people to understand and act on. This is your Challenge.
You will build a presentation about it, step by step, and deliver it at the end.
Pick something you truly care about, because it is much easier to speak well about what matters to you.

Here is the rhythm for this unit. In the old style of Global Perspectives you would 'present to the class' once and hope it went well. In the Ehel Academy model you get something better: you rehearse as many times as you like with your AI tutor, which plays your audience, asks the awkward questions and argues the other side, until your case is clear and you feel ready. Only then do you deliver it for real, to your teacher and to people at home. Rehearsing in private is exactly how nervous speakers turn into confident ones, so use it as often as you need.

bigIdeas.title: Source: Should we protect the turtle beach?
lines: Along parts of the Berbera coast, in the Horn of Africa, sea turtles come ashore at night to lay their eggs in the sand. Sea turtles are endangered, which means there are few of them left in the world.

Some people want a new rule to protect the nesting beach. They say that if the nests are left undisturbed, far more baby turtles will safely reach the sea. They add that visitors who come to watch wildlife respectfully can bring money to nearby families.

Other people are worried. Local families have used this beach for a long time, to fish and to gather. A new rule might change their daily lives, and someone would need to make sure the rule was followed, which costs time and money.

bigIdeas.title: Persuasive openers you can borrow
lines: Imagine a ... where ...
Every day, ...
Surely we all want ...
It is time to ...

Read both aloud to yourself, because a presentation is meant to be heard, not just seen on the page. If your introduction and conclusion sound clear and lively when you say them, they will work well in front of a real audience. If they sound flat or tangled aloud, that is a sign to make them shorter and simpler.

bigIdeas.title: Good questions to ask a speaker
lines: Could you explain what you mean by ...?
What do you mean by ...?
How do you know that? Where did that come from?
Can you tell me a little more about that?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Say hello to your AI tutor and tell it: I am starting Unit 6 of Global Perspectives, and the skill is Communication. This is my last unit of the year.
Ask it: In one or two simple sentences, why is it not enough to research an issue well, if I cannot communicate it?
Then tell your tutor whether you find presenting or listening harder, and why. Ask it to be your rehearsal partner for this whole unit.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor one issue you care about, then present it in three sentences: what the issue is, what you think, and one reason.
Ask the tutor to be your listener and tell you, honestly, whether it understood your issue from your three sentences.
Ask: which sentence was the clearest, and which one should I make simpler?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Pick an issue with two sides. Tell your AI tutor one argument for it and one argument against it.
Ask the tutor to play someone who holds the opposite view to yours and share their argument out loud.
Listen carefully, then tell the tutor its argument back in your own words, and ask: did I understand you correctly?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Find or recall a short source about your issue. Tell your AI tutor two arguments it makes.
For each argument, tell the tutor the supporting evidence, the fact or example that backs it up.
Ask: which of my arguments has the strongest support, and which one is a bit empty?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: List every argument you can think of for your issue to your AI tutor.
Ask the tutor to help you choose the three most persuasive ones, and to say why each is strong.
Then ask: which of my arguments would matter most to the exact people I want to reach?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your issue and your position on it.
Ask it to help you fill a skeleton plan: introduction, argument for, argument against, argument for, conclusion.
Then ask: does my order flow well, and is my one argument against stated fairly?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Present two facts about your issue to your AI tutor, and for each one, say where it came from.
Ask the tutor whether your structure was easy to follow, and where a signpost word would help.
Ask it to suggest one more source you could refer to, to make your case stronger.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your position on your issue, using the scale from strongly in favour to strongly against.
Say one plain sentence about your issue, then ask the tutor to help you make it more persuasive without changing the facts.
Ask: is my persuasive language honest, or does it stretch the truth anywhere?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor the main audience you want to influence about your issue.
Ask it to help you decide which of your arguments would matter most to that audience, and why.
Then ask the tutor to play a different audience, so you can practise leading with a different argument.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Present your whole case to your AI tutor from your skeleton plan.
Ask the tutor to tell your talk back to you: the issue, your main reasons, and your conclusion.
Whatever it misses or muddles, fix that part, then present again and see if it comes back clearer.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your introduction to your AI tutor and ask: does it name the issue, state my position, and grab attention?
Then read your conclusion and ask: does it repeat my key message and end with a clear action?
Ask the tutor to suggest one stronger final sentence for your conclusion.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor one fact and one opinion from your case, and check you have labelled each correctly.
Ask the tutor to argue the other side of your issue as strongly as it can.
Practise acknowledging its point fairly, then answering it, and ask the tutor whether your answer was convincing.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Ask your AI tutor to present a short case for a solution to a local issue, as if it were a classmate.
Listen actively and jot notes, then ask it two relevant questions: one to understand, and one to test the idea.
Ask the tutor to rate your questions and suggest one even sharper question you could have asked.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your issue, your position, and your audience.
Ask it: is my issue a good size to present in a few minutes, or is it too big?
Ask the tutor to help you say your position in one clear, confident sentence.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your arguments and supporting evidence to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether you matched the right evidence to each argument.
Then tell it the arguments for your OWN issue, and ask which ones have the strongest support.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your full list of arguments to your AI tutor.
Ask it to help you pick your three strongest, and to explain any it would choose differently.
Ask: which of my three would matter most to the audience I want to influence?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your five-part skeleton plan to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your order flows well and your argument against is stated fairly.
Ask the tutor to check that your conclusion ends with a clear, doable action.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your introduction and conclusion to your AI tutor.
Ask: does my introduction grab attention and name the issue, and does my conclusion end with a clear action?
Ask the tutor to suggest one stronger opening line and one stronger closing line.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your facts, your opinion, and your answer to the other side to your AI tutor.
Ask it to check that your facts really are facts and your opinion really is an opinion.
Ask the tutor to argue the other side back, so you can practise answering it out loud.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Present your whole case to your AI tutor from start to finish.
Ask it to be your audience and give you two stars and one wish: two things that worked and one thing to improve.
Then ask the tutor to tell your talk back to you, so you can check your key message came through clearly.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: After your listening practice, ask your AI tutor to rate your questions: were they relevant and clear?
Ask it to suggest one sharper question you could have asked.
Ask the tutor why asking How do you know that? kindly can help a whole group, not just you.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your three checkpoint sentences to your AI tutor.
Ask it: based on how my delivery went, what is one communication skill I should keep practising?
Ask the tutor to help you plan how you could communicate this same Challenge to a bigger audience one day.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your fact-or-opinion answers and your persuasive rewrites to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your rewrites stayed honest, keeping the same facts.
Ask the tutor to show you one more way to make a flat sentence persuasive.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your five answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it to tell you which answer was the strongest, and why.
Ask the tutor to give you one more scenario like these to try.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your whole-year reflection to your AI tutor.
Ask it to help you notice how much you have grown across all six skills since the start of the year.
Ask the tutor to suggest one skill to carry forward and keep sharpening, and why.

speakingPrompts.title: A human touch
lines: Ask someone at home which local issue they most wish more people understood.
Listen carefully to their answer, then tell them one issue you might present about this unit.
Bring both ideas to your next teacher session. The issues the adults around you care about often make the strongest Challenges.

speakingPrompts.title: Mina introduces her issue clearly
lines: Mina begins her talk with one clear sentence: Today I want to talk about how we travel to school, and the air we breathe on the way.
In one breath, her audience knows exactly what the issue is.
She then gives one idea at a time: first the problem, then her suggestion, then why it would help. Nobody gets lost.
Notice that clear presenting is not about big words or a loud voice. It is about order and care: knowing what you want to say, and helping the other person follow it step by step.

speakingPrompts.title: A group shares arguments for and against
lines: Mina's group is discussing whether the school should support a fund to protect the Berbera sea turtles.
Karim gives an argument for: the turtles are endangered, so protecting them helps keep them alive.
Sana gives an argument against: some families use that beach, so a new rule might make life harder for them.
Each person tells their argument, the others listen and make notes, and anyone who is unsure asks a question. By the end, the whole group understands both sides.

When you listen, you do not have to agree. You are simply trying to understand, so that later you can respond fairly. A good listener can often explain the other person's argument back to them, which is one of the surest signs that real communication has happened.

speakingPrompts.title: Leila pulls the arguments out of a source about the turtles
lines: Leila reads a short article about protecting a turtle nesting beach near Berbera.
Argument: protecting the beach helps the turtles survive. Supporting evidence: sea turtles are endangered, and more hatchlings reach the sea when nests are left undisturbed.
Argument: a protected beach can help people too. Supporting evidence: visitors who come to see wildlife can bring money to the town, and children can learn from it.
Leila also notes an argument on the other side: local families have long used the beach, so a rule would change their daily lives.

Reading a source this way makes you a sharper communicator, because you learn to separate a solid, supported argument from a weak, empty one. You will use the strongest, best-supported arguments in your own presentation.

speakingPrompts.title: Mina picks her three strongest arguments
lines: Mina has six possible arguments for walking and cycling to school. She can only use three well, so she chooses carefully.
She keeps: cleaner air to breathe, fitter and healthier children, and a safer, less crowded street.
She drops weaker ones, such as it is more fun, because they are harder to support and matter less to worried parents.
Her three chosen arguments all have facts behind them and all touch what families care about most: health and safety.

speakingPrompts.title: Mina's skeleton plan for her cycling case
lines: Introduction: how we travel to school matters for our air and our safety, and I believe more of us should walk or cycle.
Argument for: walking and cycling make no fumes, so the air near school stays cleaner.
Argument against: some children live too far away, or the road feels unsafe to walk.
Argument for: a walking bus and a safe crossing would let many more children walk safely, even from further away.
Conclusion: let us start a walking bus and ask for a crossing, so fewer cars are needed and the air is cleaner for everyone.

As you fill in your skeleton, jot down beside each point where the idea came from, so you can refer to your sources when you present. A skeleton plan turns a jumble of arguments into a clear path your audience can follow from start to finish.

speakingPrompts.title: Mina refers to her sources as she presents
lines: When Mina says the air is unhealthy, she adds: according to a health organisation, traffic fumes are bad for growing lungs.
When she says most children come by car, she adds: my own survey of twenty classmates found that eleven came by car.
By naming where each fact came from, Mina turns her opinion into a case her audience can believe.

speakingPrompts.title: Mina turns a flat sentence into a persuasive one
lines: Flat: There are a lot of cars near the school and the air is not very good.
Persuasive: Every morning our street fills with cars, and the air turns grey with fumes. Surely we all want to breathe clean air on the way to school.
Same facts, but the second version paints a picture and speaks straight to the audience, so it moves them.
Use persuasive language fairly. It should make a true idea shine, never make a false idea seem true. An honest persuader helps the audience feel what the facts already show.

speakingPrompts.title: Mina adapts her case to each audience
lines: For the school leaders, Mina leads with safety and the school's good name, because those are what they are responsible for.
For parents, she leads with their children's health and the money saved on fuel.
For other students, she leads with fresh air, fitness, and the fun of walking together in a group.
The facts stay the same. Only the order and the examples change, so each audience feels the case is about them.

speakingPrompts.title: Mina tests her structure on a listener
lines: Mina gives her talk, then asks her listener to say back its shape: what was the issue, the reasons, and the conclusion?
Her listener repeats it almost perfectly, which tells Mina her structure is clear.
When one reason gets missed, Mina knows exactly which part to make stronger, rather than guessing.

speakingPrompts.title: Mina writes her introduction
lines: Every morning, our road fills with cars, and the air turns grey with fumes. Surely we all want to breathe clean air on the way to school.
I believe that more of us should walk or cycle instead of coming by car. In the next few minutes I will explain why it is better for our health, our safety and our whole town.
Notice how Mina names the issue, states her position, and tells the audience what is coming, all in a few lively sentences.

Your conclusion is your last chance to be heard, so make it count. Repeat your key message, then finish with a clear, doable action, such as 'Let us start a walking bus next term.' An audience remembers best what they hear last.

speakingPrompts.title: Mina uses facts, opinions and the other side
lines: Fact, with a source: my survey found that eleven of twenty children came by car.
Opinion: I think our street would be calmer and kinder if more of us walked.
The other side, acknowledged: I know some families live far away, or worry the road is unsafe. That is a fair worry.
Her answer: so I am suggesting a walking bus for those nearby and a safe crossing for everyone, which meets that worry head on.
When you acknowledge the other side, use fair, respectful words: 'Some people feel ...', 'It is true that ...', 'I understand why ...'. Then answer with 'However,' or 'Even so,'.

speakingPrompts.title: Mina listens to a classmate and asks good questions
lines: Omar presents his idea that the school should let students park bicycles inside the gate.
Mina listens actively and notes two things she wants to ask.
She asks, to understand: what do you mean by a safe place to park? She asks, to test the idea: how do you know students would use it?
Omar answers, and Mina asks one follow-up to clarify. Now the whole group understands his idea far better, and so does Omar.

A powerful way to practise is to annotate as you listen: while a speaker talks, jot small notes and question marks next to the parts you want to ask about. Then your questions are ready the moment they finish. Listening and questioning like this is how a group turns many separate ideas into one shared understanding.

speakingPrompts.title: Mina's whole journey, from a smoky road to being heard
lines: Skills 1 and 2: She learned to present her issue clearly and to listen to arguments for and against.
Skills 3 and 4: She pulled arguments and evidence from her sources and chose her three strongest.
Skills 5 and 6: She built a skeleton plan and gave her talk a clear structure, referring to her survey and a health source.
Skills 7 and 8: She stated her position, used honest persuasive language, and adapted her case to each audience.
Skills 9, 10 and 11: She structured her talk for the listener, wrote a lively introduction and conclusion, and acknowledged the other side.
Skill 12: She listened to her audience's questions and answered them, and asked good questions of others in return.

By following this path, Mina turned a whole year of thinking about a smoky road into a clear, fair, persuasive case, and she delivered it to real people who could help. That is communication doing its true job: not just knowing something, but helping others understand it and act. In the Activities file, you will build and deliver your own case, one step at a time, with your AI tutor rehearsing beside you the whole way.

speakingPrompts.title: A model skeleton plan you can copy the shape of
lines: Introduction: our school rule about bicycles should change, and I am in favour of allowing safe bicycle parking.
Argument for: cycling keeps us fit and cuts the number of cars at the gate.
Argument against: some worry that bicycles could be stolen or get in the way.
Argument for: a locked rack in a corner of the yard would keep bicycles safe and tidy.
Conclusion: let us trial a bicycle rack for one term and see how it goes.

speakingPrompts.title: A model: acknowledging the other side
lines: The other side, stated fairly: it is true that some children live too far from school to walk.
The answer: however, families who live far apart could share a car, which still cuts the total number of cars.
Notice how answering the worry, instead of ignoring it, makes the case stronger and fairer.

speakingPrompts.title: Deliver it for real
lines: Bring your presentation to your next teacher session and deliver it to a real audience.
Afterwards, present it to your family or a neighbour, and ask them what they understood and what they would ask.
Write down one thing that went well, and one thing you will do even better next time.

speakingPrompts.title: Deliver it for real
lines: In your next teacher session, listen carefully to another learner's idea and ask them one relevant, kind question.
At home, ask a family member to tell you about an issue they care about, and practise asking two good questions.

starting: tell other people about an issue so they can understand it better
listen to what someone tells me about an issue and respond by asking questions
developing: presenting information on an issue using a clear structure
referring to the sources I have used
listening to what someone tells me about an issue and sharing my thoughts about their perspective
gettingBetter: listen carefully to ideas and information about an issue
respond to what others say in discussions by asking relevant questions

toolkit.title: The Communication skill, in plain words
toolkit.intro:
Communication means presenting information so that others can understand it, by speaking or writing, and also listening carefully to others and asking good questions. It has two halves that always work together: presenting your ideas clearly, and listening so you truly understand what others say back.

Two habits sit at the heart of it. First, be clear: know what you want to say, put it in a sensible order, and support it with facts and sources. Second, be fair: listen to other people, acknowledge the other side, and never pretend a whole community thinks one way. If you remember nothing else, remember those two habits.

toolkit.title: The two halves of communication
toolkit.intro: Communication is always two things at once. A strong communicator keeps swapping between them, like a good game of catch. Keep both in mind whenever you plan a presentation or take part in a discussion.

rows: Presenting
Sending your ideas out clearly, by speaking or writing.
Say what your issue is, then give one idea at a time, with an example.
Listening
Taking in what others send you, and asking about anything unclear.
Pay full attention, note the key points, then ask a relevant question.

toolkit.title: Your Stage 6 Communication learning goals
toolkit.intro: Your communication skills grow in three stages this year. Here are the real learning goals for each stage, in simple words. Your teacher may talk about these.

toolkit.title: Template: the skeleton plan
toolkit.intro: Copy this template to plan any persuasive presentation or discussion. Fill each row with your own idea, and note beside it where the idea came from, so you can refer to your sources.

rows: Introduction
Name the issue and state your position.
Argument for (+)
Your first strong reason in favour, with its support.
Argument against (-)
The other side's best point, stated fairly.
Argument for (+)
Another strong reason that answers the other side.
Conclusion
Sum up, and say the one action you want to happen.

toolkit.title: Stating your position
toolkit.intro: First place your position on this scale, then explain it with linking words that stack up your reasons.
items: The scale: strongly in favour — in favour — neutral — against — strongly against.
I am ... on this issue. This is mainly because ...
In addition ...
Furthermore ...
Finally ...

toolkit.title: Persuasive language and sentence starters
toolkit.intro:
Use these to make a true idea shine. Persuasive language should make honest ideas vivid, never make false ones seem true.

To acknowledge the other side fairly, use: It is true that ... , Some people feel ... , I understand why ... , and then answer with However, ... or Even so, ...
items: Paint a picture: Imagine a ... where ...
Speak to the audience: Surely we all want ...
Ask a question: Is this really how we want to ...?
Call for action: It is time to ... The first step is simple.
Add weight: Not only ... but also ...

toolkit.title: Facts and opinions
toolkit.intro: A strong case uses both: facts make it solid, and opinions show what you believe and why it matters. Always say where a fact came from.

rows: Fact
Something that can be checked and shown to be true.
Cars give off exhaust fumes.
Opinion
What someone thinks or believes, which others may disagree with.
Walking to school is the best way to travel.

toolkit.title: Good questions to ask a speaker
toolkit.intro:
When you listen to a presentation, respond with relevant questions. These help you understand the idea and gently test how strong it is.

Ask kindly. A good question is a gift that helps the speaker show their evidence and helps the whole group understand.
items: To understand: Could you explain what you mean by ...?
To go deeper: What do you mean by ...?
To test the idea: How do you know that? Where did that come from?
To hear more: Can you tell me a little more about that?
To reach others: What about people who ...?

toolkit.title: How to rehearse with your AI tutor
toolkit.intro:
Your AI tutor is your audience and your rehearsal partner. Use it like this, as often as you need, until your case feels clear and you feel calm.

Rehearsing in private is how nervous speakers become confident ones. Nobody sees your early, wobbly attempts except a patient tutor, so you can make all your mistakes safely, long before you stand up in front of real people.
items: Present your whole case to the tutor from start to finish, out loud if you can.
Ask it to be your audience and give you two stars and a wish: two things that worked, and one to improve.
Ask it to tell your talk back to you, so you can check that your key message came through.
Ask it to argue the other side, so you can practise answering the hard questions.
Improve one thing, then present again. Repeat until you feel ready to deliver it for real.

toolkit.title: Delivering with confidence
toolkit.intro:
When you deliver for real, in your teacher session or at home, how you speak matters as much as what you say. These simple habits help your audience listen.

You will not get all of these right at once, and that is fine. Pick just one to focus on each time you rehearse, and it will slowly become a habit you no longer have to think about.
items: Slow down. Speak a little more slowly than feels natural, so every word is clear.
Pause. Stop for a moment after your key message, to let it land.
Look up. Glance at your audience, not only at your page.
Breathe. A slow breath before you start steadies a nervous voice.
Stand tall and still. Calm hands and a steady stance help people focus on your words.

toolkit.title: Signpost words for a clear structure
toolkit.intro: Signpost words tell your audience where they are in your talk, so nobody gets lost. Sprinkle a few of these through your presentation.
items: To begin: Today I want to talk about ... , First ...
To add a reason: In addition ... , Furthermore ... , Another reason is ...
To turn to the other side: On the other hand ... , Some people feel ... , However ...
To conclude: So, to sum up ... , This is why ... , The one thing I am asking for is ...

toolkit.title: Two stars and a wish
toolkit.intro: When your AI tutor, your teacher or a family member gives you feedback, ask for it in a kind, useful shape: two stars and a wish. The two stars are two things that worked well. The wish is the one thing that would make it even better. Give feedback to others the same way. It keeps everyone brave enough to keep trying, and it always leaves the speaker with one clear thing to improve next time.

checklists.title: Checklist: Is my presentation clear and strong?
checklists.intro: Tick each one before you deliver. If you cannot tick them all, go back and improve that part.
items: Structure — it has a clear introduction, body and conclusion, in a sensible order.
Facts and opinions — I use facts I can check, and I make my own opinions clear.
Sources — I say where my facts came from.
The other side — I fairly state one argument against, and answer it.
Audience — I lead with the arguments that matter most to the people I want to influence.

challenge.intro:
You have now built and delivered a real piece of communication. Pull it together by completing these three sentences about your Challenge, in your own words:

Keep this checkpoint safe. You will look back at it during Reflection, where you will think not just about this unit, but about your whole year of six skills.
checkpoints: The message I most wanted people to understand was ...
When I delivered it, I was proud that ...
One thing I would do differently next time is ...

activities.title: Choose your issue and your position
activities.label: Activity 1: Choose your issue and your position
activities.intro:
Every presentation starts with a clear issue and a clear position. Look back at the three ideas in the Lesson file (walking or cycling to school, protecting local wildlife, or a local rule or fairness issue), or choose your own.

Choosing a clear position early makes everything easier. It does not have to be 'strongly in favour' or 'strongly against'; 'in favour, but with some worries' is an honest position too. What matters is that your audience can always tell exactly where you stand.
steps: Write your issue in one sentence: 'The issue I want to communicate is ...'.
Write your position using the scale: strongly in favour, in favour, neutral, against, or strongly against.
Write one sentence saying who you most want to influence, and why they should care.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your issue, your position, and your audience.
Ask it: is my issue a good size to present in a few minutes, or is it too big?
Ask the tutor to help you say your position in one clear, confident sentence.

activities.title: Analyse a source for arguments and evidence
activities.label: Activity 2: Analyse a source for arguments and evidence
activities.intro:
A strong case is built from strong arguments. Read the short source below about protecting a sea turtle nesting beach on the Berbera coast. Your job is to pull out its arguments and the supporting evidence for each one.

Making two columns can help: one for each argument, and one for the supporting ideas or examples beside it. A supported argument is far stronger than a bare claim.
steps: Write down two arguments FOR protecting the beach, and the supporting evidence for each.
Write down one argument AGAINST, or one worry, and the evidence or reason behind it.
Which single argument do you find the most persuasive, and why?

boxes.title: Source: Should we protect the turtle beach?
lines: Along parts of the Berbera coast, in the Horn of Africa, sea turtles come ashore at night to lay their eggs in the sand. Sea turtles are endangered, which means there are few of them left in the world.

Some people want a new rule to protect the nesting beach. They say that if the nests are left undisturbed, far more baby turtles will safely reach the sea. They add that visitors who come to watch wildlife respectfully can bring money to nearby families.

Other people are worried. Local families have used this beach for a long time, to fish and to gather. A new rule might change their daily lives, and someone would need to make sure the rule was followed, which costs time and money.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your arguments and supporting evidence to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether you matched the right evidence to each argument.
Then tell it the arguments for your OWN issue, and ask which ones have the strongest support.

activities.title: Select your most persuasive arguments
activities.label: Activity 3: Select your most persuasive arguments
activities.intro:
Now gather the arguments for your own issue and choose only the strongest. Remember, a few powerful arguments persuade better than a long list of weak ones.

It can feel strange to throw away arguments you worked hard to find. Do it anyway. An audience remembers three strong reasons far better than eight weak ones, and every weak argument you include quietly makes your strong ones look weaker too. Choosing what to leave out is one of the bravest and most useful parts of communicating well.
steps: List every argument you can think of that supports your position.
Choose the three most persuasive. For each, write why it is strong: does it have good support, does it matter to your audience, is it easy to picture?
Cross out any weak argument, and write one sentence saying why you dropped it.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your full list of arguments to your AI tutor.
Ask it to help you pick your three strongest, and to explain any it would choose differently.
Ask: which of my three would matter most to the audience I want to influence?

activities.title: Build your skeleton plan
activities.label: Activity 4: Build your skeleton plan
activities.intro:
Time to give your case its bones. A skeleton plan sets the order of your ideas so your audience can follow you. Use the five-part shape you met in the Lesson file.

Beside each point, jot where the idea came from, so you can refer to your sources when you present. Keep this skeleton plan safe: it is the frame for everything you write and say next.
steps: Introduction: write one line naming your issue and your position.
Argument for: your first strong reason in favour.
Argument against: the other side's best point, stated fairly.
Argument for: another strong reason that helps answer the other side.
Conclusion: sum up, and write the one action you want to happen.

boxes.title: A model skeleton plan you can copy the shape of
lines: Introduction: our school rule about bicycles should change, and I am in favour of allowing safe bicycle parking.
Argument for: cycling keeps us fit and cuts the number of cars at the gate.
Argument against: some worry that bicycles could be stolen or get in the way.
Argument for: a locked rack in a corner of the yard would keep bicycles safe and tidy.
Conclusion: let us trial a bicycle rack for one term and see how it goes.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your five-part skeleton plan to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your order flows well and your argument against is stated fairly.
Ask the tutor to check that your conclusion ends with a clear, doable action.

activities.title: Write your introduction and conclusion
activities.label: Activity 5: Write your introduction and conclusion
activities.intro: The introduction and the conclusion are the two parts your audience remembers most. Write them with care, using persuasive language that is vivid but honest.
steps: Write your introduction: name the issue, state your position, and open with a line that grabs attention.
Write your conclusion: repeat your key message and end with the one clear action you want.
Underline one place in each where you used persuasive language, such as a picture, a question, or a call to act.

boxes.title: Persuasive openers you can borrow
lines: Imagine a ... where ...
Every day, ...
Surely we all want ...
It is time to ...

Read both aloud to yourself, because a presentation is meant to be heard, not just seen on the page. If your introduction and conclusion sound clear and lively when you say them, they will work well in front of a real audience. If they sound flat or tangled aloud, that is a sign to make them shorter and simpler.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your introduction and conclusion to your AI tutor.
Ask: does my introduction grab attention and name the issue, and does my conclusion end with a clear action?
Ask the tutor to suggest one stronger opening line and one stronger closing line.

activities.title: Use facts and opinions, and answer the other side
activities.label: Activity 6: Use facts and opinions, and answer the other side
activities.intro: A believable case mixes facts you can check with opinions you believe, and it is brave enough to answer the other side. Build this into the body of your presentation.
steps: Write two facts that support your case, and beside each one, say where it came from.
Write one opinion of your own, starting with 'I think ...' or 'I believe ...'.
Write the strongest argument AGAINST your position, as fairly as you can.
Write your answer to it, starting with 'It is true that ...' and then 'However, ...'.

boxes.title: A model: acknowledging the other side
lines: The other side, stated fairly: it is true that some children live too far from school to walk.
The answer: however, families who live far apart could share a car, which still cuts the total number of cars.
Notice how answering the worry, instead of ignoring it, makes the case stronger and fairer.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your facts, your opinion, and your answer to the other side to your AI tutor.
Ask it to check that your facts really are facts and your opinion really is an opinion.
Ask the tutor to argue the other side back, so you can practise answering it out loud.

activities.title: Rehearse your presentation, then deliver it for real
activities.label: Activity 7: Rehearse your presentation, then deliver it for real
activities.intro:
This is the big one. Put your introduction, body paragraphs and conclusion together into one short presentation, then rehearse it fully before you deliver it. Rehearsing with your AI tutor is exactly how nerves shrink and clarity grows.

As you rehearse, practise the way you deliver, not just the words. Speak a little more slowly than feels natural, so every word is clear. Pause after your key message, to let it land. Look up at your audience instead of only at your page. And take a slow breath before you begin, because calm breathing steadies a nervous voice. Your AI tutor cannot see you, so also ask a family member to watch a run-through and tell you how you looked and sounded.
steps: Put your whole case in order, following your skeleton plan.
Read it aloud once on your own, slowly and clearly.
Rehearse it with your AI tutor as your audience, at least twice, improving it each time.
Then deliver it for real in your teacher session, and if you can, to your family at home.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Present your whole case to your AI tutor from start to finish.
Ask it to be your audience and give you two stars and one wish: two things that worked and one thing to improve.
Then ask the tutor to tell your talk back to you, so you can check your key message came through clearly.

boxes.title: Deliver it for real
lines: Bring your presentation to your next teacher session and deliver it to a real audience.
Afterwards, present it to your family or a neighbour, and ask them what they understood and what they would ask.
Write down one thing that went well, and one thing you will do even better next time.

activities.title: Practise active listening and asking questions
activities.label: Activity 8: Practise active listening and asking questions
activities.intro:
Communication is two-way, so the last activity grows your listening. You will practise active listening and asking relevant questions: the kind that help you understand and gently test an idea.

Remember that a good question is a gift, not an attack. Asking 'How do you know that?' in a kind voice helps the speaker show their evidence, and helps everyone listening decide how much to trust the idea. The best discussions, in Mogadishu, Hargeisa or anywhere else, are full of these warm, curious questions.
steps: Ask your AI tutor to present a short case for a solution to a local issue, playing a classmate.
As it speaks, annotate: jot quick notes and question marks next to anything you want to ask about.
Ask two relevant questions: one to understand (Could you explain ...?) and one to test the idea (How do you know that ...?).
Listen to the answers, then ask one follow-up question to clarify.

boxes.title: Good questions to ask a speaker
lines: Could you explain what you mean by ...?
What do you mean by ...?
How do you know that? Where did that come from?
Can you tell me a little more about that?

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: After your listening practice, ask your AI tutor to rate your questions: were they relevant and clear?
Ask it to suggest one sharper question you could have asked.
Ask the tutor why asking How do you know that? kindly can help a whole group, not just you.

boxes.title: Deliver it for real
lines: In your next teacher session, listen carefully to another learner's idea and ask them one relevant, kind question.
At home, ask a family member to tell you about an issue they care about, and practise asking two good questions.

practice.intro: Answer these in your notebook or out loud with your AI tutor. There are 15 questions. Do not worry if some are tricky; that is how you find out what to practise next. Give your own words rather than copying from the other files.
practice.prompt: In your own words, what does the word 'communication' mean?
practice.answer: Communication means presenting information so others understand it, by speaking or writing, and also listening to others and asking questions. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

practice.prompt: Communication has two halves: presenting, and ______.
practice.answer: Listening.

practice.prompt: Name the two ways you can present information to others.
practice.answer: By speaking and by writing.

practice.prompt: What is the difference between a fact and an opinion?
practice.answer: A fact can be checked and shown to be true; an opinion is what someone thinks or believes, which others may disagree with.

practice.prompt: Which of these is a fact? (a) Cars give off exhaust fumes (b) walking is the nicest way to travel (c) our town should ban cars.
practice.answer: (a) Cars give off exhaust fumes. It can be checked, so it is a fact.

practice.prompt: In a source, what is the difference between an argument and its supporting evidence?
practice.answer: An argument is the reason someone gives; the supporting evidence is the fact, detail or example that backs it up.

practice.prompt: A presenter who is good at making others agree or take action is being ______.
practice.answer: Persuasive.

practice.prompt: Put the five parts of a skeleton plan in order: conclusion, argument for, introduction, argument against, argument for.
practice.answer: Introduction, argument for, argument against, argument for, conclusion.

practice.prompt: Why does a persuasive plan include one argument against your own position?
practice.answer: Because acknowledging the other side fairly, and then answering it, makes your case fairer and more convincing, and shows you have thought about both sides.

practice.prompt: The people you are presenting to are called your ______.
practice.answer: Your audience.

practice.prompt: To change how your audience thinks or acts is to ______ them.
practice.answer: Influence.

practice.prompt: Give one reason why a presenter should refer to their sources.
practice.answer: Any one of: it proves you are not making things up; it lets your audience trust and check your work; it makes your case more believable.

practice.prompt: Write one relevant question you could ask a speaker to test how they know something.
practice.answer: Any relevant testing question, such as: How do you know that? or Where did that fact come from?

practice.prompt: What does it mean to acknowledge the other side, and why does it make your case stronger?
practice.answer: It means honestly stating what people who disagree might argue, then answering it. It makes your case stronger because it shows you are fair and have considered both sides.

practice.prompt: Name two of the six Global Perspectives skills that communication draws on.
practice.answer: Any two of: Research, Analysis, Evaluation, Reflection, Collaboration.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.intro: Match each communication word (1 to 6) to the correct meaning (A to F). Write the pairs, such as 1-C.
practice.prompt: Presenting
options: A. The people you are trying to reach when you present.
B. Sharing information so that others can understand it, by speaking or writing.
C. A reason someone gives to support their point of view.
D. To change how someone thinks or what they do.
E. Paying full attention to what others say, so you understand them.
F. Things that can be checked and shown to be true.
practice.answer: B — Sharing information so that others can understand it, by speaking or writing.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Listening
practice.answer: E — Paying full attention to what others say, so you understand them.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Argument
practice.answer: C — A reason someone gives to support their point of view.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Facts
practice.answer: F — Things that can be checked and shown to be true.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Influence
practice.answer: D — To change how someone thinks or what they do.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Audience
practice.answer: A — The people you are trying to reach when you present.

practice.intro: These short scenarios ask you to use what you have learned. Write a sentence or two for each.
practice.prompt: Sami is presenting to school leaders, and then to other students, about the same issue. Should he change his facts, or which arguments he leads with? Explain.
practice.answer: He should keep his facts the same, but change which arguments he leads with: safety for the leaders, and fresh air and fitness for the students.

practice.prompt: Nadia says: 'Everyone knows our beach is the dirtiest in the world.' Why is this weak, and how could she make it a strong, honest sentence?
practice.answer: It is an opinion dressed up as a fact, and 'the dirtiest in the world' cannot be shown to be true. A stronger version: our beach has a lot of litter, and my survey counted more than fifty pieces in one hour.

practice.prompt: Idris finishes a talk without saying what he wants to happen. Which part of his presentation is weak, and what should he add?
practice.answer: His conclusion is weak, because he never says what he wants to happen. He should add a clear, doable action, such as: let us organise a beach clean-up next month.

practice.prompt: While Layla listens to a classmate's plan, she is not sure how they know it will work. What relevant question should she ask?
practice.answer: She should ask a relevant testing question, such as: How do you know your plan will work, or where did that idea come from?

practice.prompt: Omar wants his case to feel fair. He only ever mentions arguments for his own side. What is he missing, and what should he do?
practice.answer: He is missing the other side. He should fairly state one argument against his position and then answer it, which makes his case stronger and fairer.

vocabulary.meaning: The reasons someone gives to support their point of view.
To work together with other people towards a shared goal.
Things that can be checked and shown to be true.
To change how someone thinks or what they do.
Paying full attention to what others say, so you understand them.
What someone thinks or believes, which others may disagree with.
Sharing information so that others can understand it, by speaking or writing.
Taking in information that someone else has written.
Sharing information out loud so that others can hear and understand it.
Sharing information in written words so that others can read it.
The people you are presenting to and trying to reach.
Good at making other people agree with you or take action.
A place your information comes from, such as a person, book or website.
The clear order of a presentation: beginning, middle and end.
The opening that names the issue and states your position.
The ending that sums up your case and says what you want to happen.
A simple frame that sets the order of your ideas before you present.
The point of view someone has, shaped by who they are and where they live.
Truly about the matter in hand, and therefore useful.
To make something clearer, often by asking or answering a question.

mistakes: Diving in without saying what your issue is.
Giving a long list of weak arguments instead of a few strong ones.
Sharing an opinion as if it were a checkable fact.
Using a fact but never saying where it came from.
Ignoring the other side, which makes your case look unfair.
Forgetting to end with a clear action you want to happen.
Talking so much that you never listen or ask a question.

questions.prompt: In your own words, what does the word 'communication' mean?
questions.modelAnswer: Communication means presenting information so others understand it, by speaking or writing, and also listening to others and asking questions. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

questions.prompt: Communication has two halves: presenting, and ______.
Name the two ways you can present information to others.
What is the difference between a fact and an opinion?
questions.modelAnswer: A fact can be checked and shown to be true; an opinion is what someone thinks or believes, which others may disagree with.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a fact? (a) Cars give off exhaust fumes (b) walking is the nicest way to travel (c) our town should ban cars.
questions.modelAnswer: (a) Cars give off exhaust fumes. It can be checked, so it is a fact.

questions.prompt: In a source, what is the difference between an argument and its supporting evidence?
questions.modelAnswer: An argument is the reason someone gives; the supporting evidence is the fact, detail or example that backs it up.

questions.prompt: A presenter who is good at making others agree or take action is being ______.
Put the five parts of a skeleton plan in order: conclusion, argument for, introduction, argument against, argument for.
questions.modelAnswer: Introduction, argument for, argument against, argument for, conclusion.

questions.prompt: Why does a persuasive plan include one argument against your own position?
questions.modelAnswer: Because acknowledging the other side fairly, and then answering it, makes your case fairer and more convincing, and shows you have thought about both sides.

questions.prompt: The people you are presenting to are called your ______.
To change how your audience thinks or acts is to ______ them.
Give one reason why a presenter should refer to their sources.
questions.modelAnswer: Any one of: it proves you are not making things up; it lets your audience trust and check your work; it makes your case more believable.

I can present information using a clear structure.
I can refer to the sources I have used.
I can state my position and use honest persuasive language.
